Goal. The project assistant's system prompt moves, verbatim, from C++ into the Agent page's TypeScript, is sent whole to the app over the bridge, and the app keeps no default prompt text. Kenneth's words: "we should just consolidate them in TypeScript." Do not restructure, shorten or improve the prompt's content; a later task does that, and it must start from text identical to today's so the eval can compare before and after.

Where the text is today. Two C++ literals assembled in OpenAIResponsesAgent::request_body (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp, the `instructions` string, about 850 bytes) followed by `kPrintJourneyGuidance` (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.hpp, about 1,950 bytes, three paragraphs headed "Intent and setup", "Preparation", "Verification"). The main checkout holds two uncommitted wording edits from an authorization-wording sweep that are not on origin yet; carry them so the moved text matches the main checkout: the scope sentence must read "Follow the user's requested scope; a question or a troubleshooting request is not by itself a request to change the project or to run the full preparation sequence." and the last journey sentence must read "Check the current slice before exporting G-code or sliced 3MF with export_file. The person starts a physical print with the app's Send, after its preflight; preparing a print does not start one." Everything else is moved byte for byte, including the two blank-line paragraph separators.

Why it is in C++ now, so you do not undo something deliberate: the first prompt went into C++ on 2026-09-17 (0e55c4f9be) and the journey guidance into the registry header the same day (ad2bccbee8) so the MCP server's instructions could share it. That sharing ended on 2026-10-10 (decf94b262). agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md, section "Where logic goes: the page first", already states that the text the model reads belongs on the page and holds up the printer prompt as the model. Read that section first.

The pattern to follow is the printer panel's: src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts and filamentInstructions.ts write the text; the page sends it with `printer_instructions` / `filament_instructions`; the app stores it in the session profile (AgentSessionProfile::instructions in Agent/AgentService.hpp) and sends it with every request; AgentHost::begin_reply refuses a turn that arrives with no instructions for those sessions and never falls back. A prototype of exactly this move exists, uncommitted, in the worktree at /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/action-intent-skills-routing-2136c5 (file src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts, a `project_instructions` bridge message, and the app-side refusal). Read it for the mechanism only; do not copy its prompt text, which belongs to an abandoned skills experiment, and do not bring any skill index or skill_read tool.

What to build.
- `AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts` exporting a function that returns today's prompt text (the two edits above applied), and a vitest that pins the rendered text to a fixture so an accidental change fails. The page sends it once on load and again if it changes, with a new bridge message (add it to protocol.json, AgentProtocol.hpp and protocol.ts together; the bridge version does not change, per the project's rule that additive changes go in the capabilities list).
- The app stores it in the project session's profile and sends it as `instructions`. Delete the C++ literals and `kPrintJourneyGuidance`; update the unit test in tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp that pins the guidance substring to instead check that the request carries exactly what the page sent. The MCP server's own four-sentence instructions in Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp and the conversation-title prompt stay in C++ (MCP has no page; the title request is the app's own).
- A project turn that arrives before the page has sent instructions must not be sent with empty or default text. A typed turn comes from the page, so it cannot arrive first. An app-started turn can: the note after a file opens (AgentHost::on_file_loaded) starts a turn, and the app may open a file before the page has loaded. Queue that turn until the instructions arrive rather than dropping it; say in the report how you verified the race. The file-report skill (fileReportInstructions.ts, sent as `file_report_instructions`) is separate and stays as it is.
- Update the docs: the architecture.md table row for the project prompt if there is one, and agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md where it names `kPrintJourneyGuidance` (grep for it; near "intent_update and plan_set are in-app only").
- Keep the instructions byte-identical across requests of a conversation; the provider cache depends on it.

Other tasks in flight on the same base also edit AgentHost.cpp (one removes the explain-only tool switch in make_agent_request and handle_agent_tool_call; one renames ToolExecutionCoordinator::propose to submit; one removes the unsaved-work refusals in the coordinator). Keep your AgentHost changes to begin_reply, the new bridge message handler and the session profile, so the merges stay small.

Run the shell harness default scenario so a real page sends the instructions and a live request body shows them, with no model call. Do not call any live model.

64-## Production integration boundaries
65-
66-### Shell host
67-
68-The shell is the JusPrin window frame around OrcaSlicer's content. Build one shell, in files this fork owns, and attach it to `MainFrame` in one small place. Decisions about what happens at startup go in a bootstrap or a shell factory that the fork owns. Do not spread environment checks through OrcaSlicer's constructors.
69-
70-The first production version may still construct OrcaSlicer's old top bar, tab panel, Sidebar, and `GUI_ObjectList` where existing OrcaSlicer behavior depends on them. Leave them out of the visible layout. Do not hide them behind a separate top-level window. Stopping them from being constructed at all is a separate project, because it changes object lifetimes.
71-
72-### Build registration
73-
74-List JusPrin's source files explicitly in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/sources.cmake`. OrcaSlicer's central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt` should pull that file in with one include line that never changes. The fork should not keep adding its own files to OrcaSlicer's list.
75-
76-### Workspace boundary
77-
78-The workspace API is the typed C++ interface JusPrin uses to read and change the project. The production version should keep the ideas from the proof of concept (POC) that worked:
79-
80-- separate types for plate IDs and object IDs, so one cannot be passed where the other is expected;
81-- read-only snapshots of the project;
82-- explicit errors from commands;
83-- typed reasons that say what kind of change happened;
84-- a revision number that only goes up;
85-- subscriptions that end automatically when the object holding them is destroyed, and that can be moved but not copied.
86-
87-Before production use, the API must also:
88-
89-- say which calls must run on the GUI thread;
90-- say exactly when the revision number goes up;
91-- explicitly mark the old session's IDs invalid when a project is replaced;
92-- notice changes that did not go through the adapter (the JusPrin class that implements this API on top of OrcaSlicer);
93-- report undo and redo availability whether or not any particular widget is visible;
94-- report whether an undo or redo really changed OrcaSlicer's state;
95-- not depend on `GUI_ObjectList` for commands that change the model;
96-- offer plate selection, object import and addition, and the other commands the product needs;
97-- keep wxWidgets types and OrcaSlicer types out of its public interface.
98-
99-Sometimes the operation you need exists only inside OrcaSlicer's UI code. In that case, add the smallest possible command to the OrcaSlicer class that already does the work, and name it for what it does. Do not copy the operation into JusPrin. Do not fake clicks or key presses on hidden controls.
100-
101-### Canvas presentation
102-
103-`GLCanvas3D` keeps a small API for controlling how its parts are presented. That API contains nothing specific to JusPrin. A controller in fork-owned code uses the API to apply JusPrin's choices, and puts OrcaSlicer's previous state back when the controller is destroyed. Whether a control is drawn and whether it receives input must be two separate switches. Otherwise a control that is hidden could still swallow pointer events. OrcaSlicer's native gizmos (the on-canvas tools such as Move and Rotate) must stay usable while one is active.
104-
105-The POC had one broad switch, `render_overlays`. Production needs finer control. Treat each of these as its own item that can be shown or hidden separately: OrcaSlicer's main toolbar, the gizmo picker, the handles of the active gizmo, plate actions, object labels, layer-editing controls, navigation aids, the Preview legend, and the Preview sliders. Some controls are shared between canvases, such as `Plater`'s collapse toolbar. A shared control must be saved and restored by one object that lives as long as the shell does. Do not give each canvas its own guard for it.
106-
107-### Plates and Project pane
108-
109-This pane is native code owned by the fork (`Shell/LeftPane`). It sits to the left of the workspace on Prepare. Its first tab lists every plate, even when the project has only one. Its second tab shows the saved project's identity, the model's 3MF metadata, the history of physical prints, the version history, and export. The pane keeps no project state of its own and has no undo of its own. It draws what two model classes describe, and those classes do not depend on the GUI. Every click calls a workspace command.
110-
111-| Piece | What it is responsible for |
112-|---|---|
113-| `Workspace/ProjectOutline.hpp`, `IWorkspace::outline()` | The data the pane reads: plates, copies of objects (each with the plate that holds it), volumes, facts about customization and the mesh, and what is selected below the object level. Which plate a copy is on comes from `PartPlateList`. The code never guesses it from where the copy sits. |
114-| `Shell/LeftPaneModel` | Which rows the Plates tab shows, and when. The active plate is open. Other plates are folded, each with a summary computed from its current copies. A row has child rows only when there is data for them. "Not on a plate" appears only when some copy is on no plate. This class also handles switching between the tabs and between the views inside the Project tab. |
115-| `Shell/ProjectPaneModel` | The contents of the Details and Print history views, as plain data. A field that nobody filled in is left out. The slicer's time estimate and the measured print duration are kept as separate values. A ledger record that has nothing to display is included in the count but gets no row. |
116-| `Workspace/OrcaOutline.cpp` | The commands, implemented on top of OrcaSlicer: `select_plate`, `add_plate`, `select_copy`, `select_volume`, `plate_actions`, `run_plate_action`. Each command ends by calling the same code OrcaSlicer's own UI calls (`Plater::select_plate_by_hover_id`, the toolbar's Add plate event, `Selection` plus the canvas's object-select event). The events are raised synchronously on the GUI thread, so the change has already happened when the command returns. |
117-| `Shell/LeftPane`, `LeftPaneProject.cpp` | Drawing and input. While drawing, the pane records where each control ended up. Pointer handling looks each click up in that record, so a click can only hit something that was actually drawn. |
118-
119-The ledger is the record of physical prints. It can have any number of subscribers, through `ProjectPersistence::subscribe_ledger`. The pane and the header's overflow menu each subscribe to it separately.
120-
121-### Print issues and OrcaSlicer's notifications
--
166:#### Where logic goes: the page first
167-
168-When the same logic could live either in C++ or in a React page, put it in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++. The page is quicker to change: Vite hot-reloads it, while a C++ change means relinking a multi-gigabyte GUI library. The page's tests run in milliseconds under Vitest. The text people read is already written in the page. The text the model reads belongs there too.
169-
170-Strong reasons for C++:
171-
172-- **It reads or changes OrcaSlicer state:** presets, the model, plates, slicing, the device list. The page never owns project state (see the constraints below).
173-- **The app has to guarantee it.** This covers what a tool accepts and refuses, which tools a session may call, and what is sent to the model provider (API keys, access codes, project data). Page code can describe a limit, but only the app can enforce one.
174-- **It has to work without a page:** the MCP server, background work, tests that run without a browser.
175-- **It needs a thread the page does not have, or has to stay alive at times when the page is not.**
176-
177-The printer panel shows how this works. The app sends the page only facts: sizes, spools, which printer a card shows, and what a change altered. The page turns those facts into all of the text:
178-
179-- The page writes the model's instructions in `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` and sends them to the app with `printer_instructions`.
180-- The page writes the panel's own text in `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts`. That is the opening line and the note that goes with each tap. The opening line is sent with `printer_opening`. The note for a tap is sent inside that tap's payload.
181-
182-The app's part:
183-
184-- It decides which tools the model gets: the five printer tools and the four settings tools, the same list in every mode.
185-- It checks every tool call.
186-- It refuses a call that does not fit the conversation. Examples are adding a printer outside an Add conversation, changing a printer other than the one the conversation is about, and changing a setting on anything other than that printer.
187-- It refuses a turn that arrives with no instructions. It does not fall back to the project assistant's prompt.
188-- It posts the opening line once per session.
189-- It posts the note for a tap only when the tap goes through, and limits the note to 2 KB.
190-- It still writes the notes for things only the app can find out when the tap arrives: the network printer has gone, the printer's model id is not on the list, or a save or an undo failed.
191-
192-Windows uses WebView2, macOS uses WKWebView, and Linux uses WebKitGTK. The way the page's files are packaged must work on all three. The prototype packed the whole page into a single local file, because WKWebView failed to load additional files referenced through `file:` URLs. Production keeps the single-file approach, and CMake now builds that file from the TypeScript/React sources.
193-
194-MCP (Model Context Protocol, which lets external AI tools call the app) and wider agent autonomy are layers that come after this one. They must go through the same typed workspace interface. They must not change who owns the 3D view.
195-
196-### Gizmo presentation
197-
198-Start with Move or Rotate. Build one reusable native controller that wraps the existing behavior:
199-
200-1. Show a compact strip of tool buttons in the upper-left corner of the Prepare canvas. The strip is a horizontal row like OrcaSlicer's own toolbar, but aligned to the left instead of centred. The strip stays put when the selection or the camera moves, because a strip attached to the object would jump every time the view orbits. `Canvas/ViewportToolStrip` draws the strip with ImGui as part of the canvas's own frame, through `GLCanvas3D::set_overlay_renderer`. On every frame it asks the gizmo manager which tool is open. The open tool's values appear below the row in `Canvas/ToolValuePanel`, lined up with the button that opened the tool.
201-2. Activate the existing native gizmo.
202-3. Keep the existing pointer dragging, snapping, and selection behavior.
203-4. Send exact typed-in numbers through `GizmoObjectManipulation`.
204-5. Keep the existing timing of undo snapshots, and the existing undo and redo.
205-6. Closing a tool only closes it. Do not invent a draft that can be thrown away. Undo stays the way to revert a change, unless the product requirements explicitly change that.
206-
207-After that, convert the remaining tools in groups that work in a similar way: Move/Rotate/Scale; Mirror/Duplicate/Place on face; Measure; Cut/Repair; Text/Emboss; painter-based tools.
208-
209-### Semantic annotations
210-
211-Semantic annotations are labels a person puts on part of a model to say what that part means, such as a face that must stay smooth. Reuse what OrcaSlicer's painting tools already do: raycasting, brush selection, clipping, showing painted facets, copying, undo, and saving into the 3MF file. Two things are not yet proven for production: labels with arbitrary meanings, and how those labels are presented to the agent. The first implementation should use two labels on one object. Before adding more labels, check that those two survive save and reload, transforms, duplication, undo and redo, and changes to the mesh's topology.
212-
213-## Non-negotiable constraints
214-
215-- Do not change slicing algorithms to make the UI easier to build.
216-- Do not replace `GLCanvas3D` or the G-code Preview.
217-- Do not reimplement geometry operations in TypeScript.
218-- Do not place WebView content over the native GL canvas.
219-- Do not keep a second copy of the project model or of the undo stack in JavaScript.
220-- Preserve 3MF projects, printer profiles, shortcuts, serialization, and cross-platform behavior.
221-- Do not try to match every stock OrcaSlicer feature when the product definition does not require it.
222-- Do not reopen the Electron or WebGL question without a new, explicit product decision backed by evidence.

Every build of the fork (and /Applications/OrcaSlicer.app) shares bundle id `com.softfever3d.orca-slicer`. The desktop-control tools resolve an app by bundle id and bind to whichever instance comes first, so `app_list_windows` returns `[]` and filtered screenshots hide the window you actually launched.

**Working recipe (2026-09-05):** `ditto` the built .app into the scratchpad, `plutil -replace CFBundleIdentifier -string com.jusprin.worktree-test`, `codesign --force --deep -s -`, then `open -n <copy>.app --args <model>` and `request_access` for the new id. `app_screenshot`/`app_click` then work and include popup menus. A display-scope `left_click` on the header did NOT open the fork's PopupWindow menus, but a background `app_click` did; take the pixel-level `zoom` with the display tools afterwards (call `app_release` first). Display-scope `Escape` does not close those popups; a click elsewhere does.

The MCP discovery file `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/mcp.json` points at the newest instance's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`; `tests/mcp/probe.py`'s `call()` can drive real tools (e.g. `workspace_inspect`, then `report_slice_review` with sessionId/plateId/sliceResultId) to put the header into the Check-print state without lldb. lldb `expr` cannot call inline accessors like `status_row()`.

**Why:** On 2026-09-01 a verification pass screenshotted the stock app instead of the build; on 2026-09-05 the tools bound to another session's main-repo build.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
concluding anything about the app.
